title: India Has Slipped From the World's Fourth-Largest Economy to Sixth. The Opposition Just Published the Receipts.
excerpt: Congress released a 76-page report card on Modi 3.0's second year. The findings: a record-low rupee, 8 per cent fuel hikes, capital flight, and a fiscal deficit heading toward 5 per cent.
body:
India has slipped from the world's fourth-largest economy to the sixth. The rupee has hit an all-time low of 96.97 against the dollar. Petrol and diesel prices are up 8 per cent. Cooking gas subsidies have been cut. Capital is fleeing.

These are not opposition talking points. They are data points, pulled from a 76-page report card that the Indian National Congress released this week on the second year of Modi 3.0. The document, titled "Promise vs Reality: Year 2 of Modi 3.0," represents the most detailed economic indictment the opposition has assembled since the current government returned to power in 2024.

The Numbers Tell the Story

The centrepiece of the Congress critique is India's slide in the global economic rankings. After years of climbing the ladder — reaching fourth place in 2025 — India has now fallen back to sixth, behind Japan and Germany. The Congress report attributes this to a combination of the rupee's depreciation, weak private investment, record foreign capital outflows and a government it says failed to build resilience during the years when global oil prices were low.

Rajeev Gowda, a senior Congress leader and former member of the Reserve Bank of India's central board, made the case bluntly: "Please don't do that. Swallow that bitter pill for a little while because you have been enjoying the fruits." He was addressing the government's decision to pass higher crude oil costs on to consumers rather than absorb them through fiscal buffers — buffers he says the government could have built during years of cheap energy but chose instead to tax.

State-owned fuel retailers have raised petrol and diesel prices by roughly 8 per cent since the Iran war began disrupting global energy supplies in February. The government has simultaneously cut subsidies on cooking gas cylinders for households — a move that hits rural and lower-income families hardest.

Fiscal Cracks Widening

The report lands at a moment when India's fiscal position is under unusual strain. The government is targeting a fiscal deficit of 4.3 per cent of GDP this year, but a Reuters poll of economists forecast it would swell to 4.7 per cent, with some projections reaching 5 per cent.

India's fertiliser ministry has already requested a doubling of its subsidy budget, barely three months into the financial year. Fertiliser is vital for India's agrarian economy, which supports nearly half the population — and the risk of drought from the strengthening El Nino makes the stakes even higher.

The government has also cut gasoline and diesel taxes, forgoing 140 billion rupees in monthly revenue. A 1.2 trillion rupee (roughly $12.6 billion) support package for oil refiners and retailers — compensation for not hiking pump prices during the first 78 days of the war — has added to the fiscal burden.

The Diaspora Dimension

For the roughly 32 million Indians living abroad, the report's findings have immediate relevance. The rupee's record weakness means that the dollar value of Indian assets — property, mutual funds, bank deposits — has eroded significantly. A family that bought a flat in Mumbai for 1 crore rupees when the dollar was at 83 has seen its dollar-denominated value drop by more than 15 per cent.

Remittances, which hit a record $43.5 billion in a single quarter earlier this year, are worth more in rupee terms — a silver lining for families receiving money from abroad. But for NRIs contemplating investments in India, the currency weakness introduces risk that even the RBI's new deposit schemes cannot fully offset.

The Congress report also highlights India's unemployment crisis, capital outflows and what it calls a breakdown in investor confidence. Private investment remains weak, and the foreign portfolio investor exodus — driven by a combination of geopolitical risk, currency weakness and high U.S. yields — has been the most severe in India's market history.

The Government's Response

Oil Minister Hardeep Singh Puri pushed back on Monday, saying India expected oil and gas prices to drop in the coming months and that the country had adequate stocks despite the war. A senior government official separately insisted that capital expenditure would not be pulled back and that economic growth was not yet under stress, citing strong domestic consumption.

But the opposition's report, whatever its political motivations, compiles data that economists have been flagging for weeks. India's credit rating agency Crisil warned that higher transport costs from fuel price hikes would "reverberate across the economy through higher food and core inflation." Goldman Sachs, while capping its rupee depreciation forecast, has been careful to note that the fundamental pressures remain unresolved.

The Congress party under Rahul Gandhi has struggled to convert economic anxiety into political momentum. But this report — detailed, data-heavy and timed to coincide with the rupee's continued fragility — represents an attempt to reframe the national conversation around the gap between the government's economic narrative and the numbers that underpin it.
